findings.exact_text: The bridge was dropping, and the line, still clipped to his harness and pulled taut by the falling span, dragged him backward.
findings.reason: The line was tied to a trunk and held by Nisa, not attached to the bridge, so the falling span could not pull it taut. Cutting it is then unnecessary.

findings.exact_text: Cutting the line had saved him.
findings.reason: Cutting is framed as the rescue, but the line is not shown connected to the falling bridge, so the causal claim is unsupported.

findings.exact_text: he cut the line from his harness
findings.reason: The line was tied to a trunk and Nisa caught its free end; the harness clip is not established. Cutting the line also strands it with the bridge.

findings.exact_text: Their gliders still lay on the shore, waiting.
findings.reason: Nisa's glider landing is never shown, and the gliders were never staked down against the wind and mist.

findings.exact_text: found the great root span still hooked to its far anchor, its near anchor torn loose
findings.reason: They approach from the camp and Arda crossed the bridge heading inland, so near and far anchors and sides are confused with the later rescue.

findings.exact_text: "I'll be back soon; if the light starts to dim, that's our signal to turn back.
findings.reason: Nisa says she will return soon, and her promise is oddly repeated; it conflicts with S082's 'we promised... careful' tone. Minor timing and wording mismatch.
Narration in close third person hedges awkwardly with 'presumably' and 'certainly'.

findings.exact_text: It was not like any pattern he'd ever seen.
findings.reason: Redundant with the preceding sentence 'not any pattern currently taught'; also 'almost recognized' contradicts it.

findings.exact_text: Arda brought the glider in at an angle, half-flying and half-falling
findings.reason: Minor: the beats call for the rope to be the cut climax, but its tie-off logic deviates from the spine's rescue-line role.

findings.exact_text: but not any pattern currently taught
findings.reason: “Not any pattern” is an unnatural determiner construction here; idiomatic English uses “not one currently taught.”

findings.exact_text: not like any pattern he'd ever seen
findings.reason: A hitch more naturally “matches” a pattern; “was not like any pattern” sounds imprecise and slightly non-native.
The repeated “with” and intervening comma awkwardly separate two parallel things filling the pages.

findings.exact_text: you got off it in time
findings.reason: “Got off” gives an unclear physical relationship to the line; “cut yourself free” directly and naturally describes the action.

target_segments.source_text: Arda brought the glider in at an angle, half-flying and half-falling, and a root caught the skid and tilted it sideways.
A length of bleached rope ran around the trunk, half-sunk into bark that had grown over it, tied in a hitch he almost recognized—a guild-style anchor, but not any pattern currently taught.
It was not like any pattern he'd ever seen.
Somewhere behind them, back past the shore, the corridor they'd flown through was, presumably, still open, though its light had not yet begun to dim.
"I'll be back soon; if the light starts to dim, that's our signal to turn back.
Someone should look at the sky while you chase knots." She was already climbing, and he knew she'd come find him once she'd seen it.
The pages were filled with strong, practical handwriting, with sketches of these same knots.
They hurried back toward the bridge they had crossed.

They came down through the mist-filled trees at a dead run and found the great root span still hooked to its far anchor, its near anchor torn loose, thrashing in the wind above a drop into the cloud sea.
He tied one end to the last living trunk on his side, swung the free end across the gap, and Nisa caught it and hauled herself across hand over hand while the wind tried to peel her off.
The bridge was dropping, and the line, still clipped to his harness and pulled taut by the falling span, dragged him backward.
There was only one thing left to do, and he hated every second of it: he cut the line from his harness and let it fall away with the bridge.
Cutting the line had saved him.
"Your line," Nisa agreed quietly, "and you got off it in time."
Their gliders still lay on the shore, waiting.
